title: Follow me (Mark 1:14–20)
hook: Mark's favorite word: immediately they left their nets

segments.voice: Yesterday: schizō, the heavens torn open, a voice saying beloved, and then the desert. Your line was beloved, then the desert.

Early morning on the Sea of Galilee. It's really a lake, and the fishing is hard work: nets, boats, cold water, a family business. Two brothers, Simon and Andrew, stand in the shallows casting a net. A man walks along the shore. He stops, looks at them, and says two words, more or less: follow me. Down the beach, it happens again, with two more brothers, James and John, mending nets in their father's boat. The opposite of what they do is familiar: meant to, planned to, will get to it. And Mark's word for what they did is the heartbeat of his whole gospel.
screen: `EARLY MORNING ON THE LAKE.` → `TWO BROTHERS CASTING A NET.` → `FOLLOW ME.`

segments.voice: Immediately. In Greek, euthys. Mark uses it again and again; read him in one sitting and it's everywhere. The King James Bible often says straightway. Once you notice it, you can't stop: straightway he saw the heavens torn, immediately the Spirit drove him out, and now this. First, the scene. John the Baptist has been arrested. Jesus comes into Galilee announcing: "The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand: repent ye, and believe the gospel." Repent, in Mark's Greek, is about a change of mind, a new direction. Then the lake. He sees Simon and Andrew casting a net, and says: "Come ye after me, and I will make you to become fishers of men." A fisherman's joke, almost: you catch fish now, you'll catch people. "And straightway they forsook their nets, and followed him." No negotiation, no three-month notice. A little further on, James and John are in their boat with their father, Zebedee. Jesus calls them, and they leave their father in the boat with the hired men, and go. Mark doesn't say what they were thinking, or whether they'd met Jesus before; John's gospel suggests some of them had. He just shows the speed. Readers notice the cost, too: a father left sitting in a boat. For Mark, immediately is not recklessness. It's the rhythm of a story where God's time has arrived and can't wait. Some readers hear it as a question: what's the net in my hands, and what would it mean to put it down?
screen: `EUTHYS — AGAIN AND AGAIN.` · `THE TIME IS FULFILLED.` · `FISHERS OF MEN.` · `A FATHER LEFT IN THE BOAT.` · then, large: `STRAIGHTWAY THEY FORSOOK THEIR NETS.`

segments.voice: Think of one small, good thing you've been putting off: texting a friend who's struggling, apologizing, signing up to help, returning the call, opening the Bible you meant to open. Notice the net in your hands, the reasons, the timing, the someday, and picture putting it down and doing the thing. If you pray, you can ask for the nerve to do it today.
Immediately. In Greek, euthys. Mark's word, again and again, the heartbeat of a story that won't wait.
Your line: leave the nets. Straightway they forsook them, and followed. That's day one hundred fifty-nine.

howItsDone: Many Christians read the calling of the first disciples as a call to their own lives, and churches often read it when commissioning people for new work or ministry.

trapdoor: what you thought: immediately just means quickly.
what it means: Mark's heartbeat word. God's time has come, and the story moves before anyone can stall.
what a scholar hears: euthys, repeated so often in Mark that it can work as a connective, 'and then', as much as a word for speed.
